The Google Cloud Data Analytics, BI, and Database teams

Recent product news and updates from our data analytics, database and business intelligence teams.

October 19 - October 23

  • BigQuery introduces column aliases in GoogleSQL and cross-region table copy GA

    GoogleSQL in BigQuery now supports column aliases in 

    SELECT
    and 
    WHERE
    clauses (GA opt-in), avoiding nested subqueries and simplifying migrations from Snowflake and Teradata. Cross-region table copying is also now generally available to streamline regional data replication and disaster recovery. Review the BigQuery release notes.

  • Conversational analytics in BigQuery expands to Canada and adds CSV/PDF export

    Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now available in Montréal (

    northamerica-northeast1
    ) and Toronto (
    northamerica-northeast2
    ) to support Canadian data residency requirements. You can also now export agent responses — including text, tables, charts, and citations — directly to CSV or PDF (GA). Learn more about conversational analytics in BigQuery.

  • AlloyDB Omni 18.4.0 is now GA with Advanced Query Insights and external KMS support

    AlloyDB Omni 18.4.0 brings PostgreSQL 18.4 to self-hosted and multi-cloud environments, adding the 

    google_insights_v2
    extension for granular query execution and wait-event diagnostics. It also adds Thales CipherTrust Manager support for Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) alongside HashiCorp Vault. Explore the AlloyDB Omni release notes.

  • Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL adds managed connection pooling and Private Service Connect defaults

    Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL now supports enabling built-in managed connection pooling on existing Private Service Connect (PSC) instances to scale high-concurrency workloads. PSC is also now the default private IP option for new Cloud SQL instances in new projects to simplify cross-project networking. Review Cloud SQL updates.

  • Customer momentum: Unico prevents over $5B in fraud on Google's Agentic Data Cloud

    Digital identity platform Unico migrated from Databricks Spark/Scala clusters to BigQuery and Spanner at the core of its data architecture. Unifying real-time transaction streams with petabyte-scale analytics enabled low-latency identity verification that has prevented over $5 billion in fraud. Read the Unico case study.

  • Developer guide: Getting started with Looker Data Apps

    Following the debut of Looker Data Apps in preview, a new walkthrough on the Google Developer Community shares practical patterns for building prompt-driven applications inside Looker. Read the guide on the Google Developer Community.

October 12 - October 16

  • Looker Data Apps are now in Preview to build and host interactive, agent-generated applications natively inside Looker

    Generated using natural language prompts, the Antigravity CLI, or Claude Code, these interactive web applications, natively hosted inside Looker, transform business reporting into operational systems of action. Users can test scenarios, adjust parameters, and trigger workflows in downstream platforms while inheriting LookML semantic modeling, row-level security, and access controls with no runtime LLM token costs. Read the announcement blog.

  • Build end-to-end data science pipelines with the Data Agent Kit

    Following the general availability of the Data Agent Kit, a new end-to-end walkthrough demonstrates how data teams can build, test, and schedule machine learning pipelines directly from their preferred code editors. Explore the walkthrough and codelab.

  • Manage dashboard agents as code to bring CI/CD and version control to LookML dashboards

    Data teams can now declare agent parameters, configurations, and prompt instructions alongside dashboard files in code. This integration enables standard developer workflows for conversational BI, including Git version control, peer review, branching, and automated CI/CD validation before agent modifications reach production end users. Read the technical guide on the Google Developer Community.

  • Simplify AI search with native AlloyDB hybrid search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion

    AlloyDB for PostgreSQL simplifies hybrid search architectures by combining vector similarity search and keyword BM25 retrieval within a unified database engine. Using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), developers can merge lexical scoring and semantic embeddings into a single ranked result without writing a complex SQL query. This unified approach removes the operational overhead of running and synchronizing external search engines alongside operational databases for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and search applications.Explore hybrid search in AlloyDB.

October 5 - October 9

  • Data Agent Kit is now generally available to bring Google Data Cloud to any coding agent

    Data Agent Kit provides a free collection of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and Google-authored agent skills that connect more than 15 Google Data Cloud services directly to coding agents across VS Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. This release expands support for developers and data practitioners to inspect schemas, author queries, and build end-to-end data pipelines in natural language directly from their IDE or CLI. Read the announcement blog.

  • Spanner Omni is now generally available for deploy-anywhere, multi-model workloads

    Spanner Omni brings Spanner's distributed SQL, graph, vector, and key-value capabilities to any environment, including on-premises data centers, other public clouds via Kubernetes or VMs, and local developer laptops. Organizations can build and run multi-model applications with consistent APIs and query engines across hybrid and multi-cloud footprints while seamlessly scaling to managed Spanner on Google Cloud. Read the launch blog and explore how Spanner also removed cumulative mutation limits for DML transactions.

  • AlloyDB delivers PostgreSQL for agents and native BM25 hybrid search

    We announced PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB, introducing an agentic database architecture engineered for real-time data access at agent scale with workload isolation. In addition, native BM25 ranking is now in Preview for AlloyDB and Cloud SQL, allowing developers to combine keyword search and vector embeddings directly in PostgreSQL without maintaining an external search engine. For hybrid deployments, the AlloyDB Omni RPM Orchestrator is now generally available, and you can dive deeper in our new Build AI apps and agents with AlloyDB eBook.

  • Lakehouse runtime catalog adds regional endpoints across 22 regions and GA support for flexible column names

    Lakehouse runtime catalog regional endpoints are now live across 22 Google Cloud regions across the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East, supporting both the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint and the Apache Hive catalog endpoint to help customers meet strict data residency and sovereignty requirements. In addition, flexible column names for Apache Iceberg tables are now generally available by default across Iceberg external tables and managed tables, enabling seamless querying of columns containing spaces, hyphens, and Unicode characters. We also announced the Preview of cross-cloud caching and connections for the borderless Lakehouse.

  • Unlock predictive and agent-ready insights with BigQuery augmented analytics TVFs, TabFM, and identity columns

    BigQuery introduced augmented analytics table-valued functions (TVFs): six built-in functions that automate metric diagnostics, trend analysis, and pattern discovery directly where your data lives and integrate as skills for AI agents. We also introduced TabFM in BigQuery to bring tabular foundation model capabilities to predictive analytics, alongside BigQuery identity columns to automatically generate sequential surrogate keys and simplify data warehouse pipelines.

  • Dataflow adds Pause/Resume and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU support for large-scale AI workloads

    New Dataflow capabilities make it easier to run high-throughput streaming and batch AI pipelines at scale, including Pause/Resume job controls and support for NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. And for teams running Apache Spark workloads, learn how to mitigate compute stockouts and maximize availability using flexible VMs.

  • Unlock up to 3x higher QPS and microsecond latency with Memorystore for Valkey 9.1

    Memorystore for Valkey 9.1 is now available, delivering up to 3x higher queries per second (QPS) and microsecond-level caching latencies to accelerate high-throughput applications and real-time AI agent state management. Read the blog.

  • Customer momentum across Google Data Cloud — Yahoo, PayPal, Surescripts, Airwallex, and Lucius AI

    Organizations across industries are scaling their data and AI foundations on Google Data Cloud. Yahoo uses flexible VMs in Managed Service for Apache Spark to reduce provisioning failures by 85%, while PayPal migrated mission-critical analytics workloads to Managed Service for Apache Spark to scale and reduce operational overhead. On the database front, Surescripts migrated 30.5 billion annual healthcare transactions to AlloyDB with 99.998% uptime, Airwallex manages more than 5,000 databases with 99.99% availability on Cloud SQL with a team of four DBAs, and Lucius AI runs a 210,000-tender global platform on AlloyDB and MCP with 47x faster ScaNN vector search.

September 7 - September 10

  • Pub/Sub SMTs can now AI Inference your Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models!

    Pub/Sub AI Inference SMTs allow you to apply inference on an incoming stream of events using models hosted in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The model’s prediction is appended to your event, making it available for downstream processing in your data warehouse (like BigQuery) or operational database (like BigTable). This feature, now generally available, can dramatically simplify or enhance anomaly detection systems you are operating. 

  • PostgreSQL Source Connector is now generally available in Managed Service for Apache Kafka!

    Managed Service for Apache Kafka’s PostgreSQL connector allows customers to capture changes from their PostgreSQL database and ingest them into their Kafka infrastructure with low latency. This source connector is compatible withCloud SQL for Postgres, AlloyDB, and self-managed PostgreSQL databases. Try this along with our entire portfolio of managed connectors, including MirrorMaker 2.0, BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and Pub/Sub! E-mail kafka-hotline@google.com if you have questions or feedback!

  • Pause-on-failure for Dataflow batch jobs is GA

    Dataflow pause-on-failure enables you to preserve the state of a batch Dataflow job before it fails. By pausing your Dataflow job, you can address issues that are external to the pipeline and resume processing without losing completed work. This helps you better manage resource costs and improve job reliability when you face temporary outages or capacity constraints.

  • The insertAll API is now the BigQuery Storage Write API (REST)

    The legacy insertAll streaming API is now rebranded as the BigQuery Storage Write API (REST). By dropping the "legacy" label, developers can confidently build long-term HTTP-based streaming workflows. This stateless JSON-over-HTTPS endpoint offers a lightweight alternative to heavy gRPC libraries—ideal for serverless web apps, IoT telemetry, and AI logging. The transition is seamless for existing users, requiring zero code changes and offering 100% backward compatibility. However, the Storage Write API (gRPC) version remains the recommended standard for high-throughput, continuous pipelines.

August 31 - September 4

  • Stateful processing is available in BigQuery continuous queries in Preview

    Stateful operations significantly expand what’s possible with BigQuery continuous queries. This feature allows users to leverage functions like 
    JOIN
    s, aggregations, and windowing functions directly in their streaming queries. Now you can calculate metrics over time (for example, a 30-minute average) to power your downstream applications and AI agents with much richer, real-time signals.

    Try out our featurehere and share your feedback with bq-continuous-queries-feedback@google.com!

  • Synthetic data generator tool is available for Managed Service for Kafka

    You’ve launched your first Kafka cluster. Now what? The next thing to do is to produce some data to the cluster, but that involves modifying a client application somewhere or spinning up a virtual machine. The synthetic data generator tool, now generally available, can start sending mock data to your cluster in 3 clicks, and will get data streaming into your cluster in less than two minutes. The perfect utility for those moments you just want to test your cluster and new features. Try our quickstart today!

  • Dataflow pipeline updates are faster & more flexible

    Dataflow pipeline updates can now stop-and-replace pipelines, a major addition to the existing in-place-update feature. The new parallel pipeline option accelerates the migration between the old & new pipeline, resulting in reduced disruption to your business. You can also set a timeout on drains that prevents runaway costs for your pipeliness in the event of stuck processing. This feature is generally available. Try it here!

July 6 - July 10

  • New Lakehouse managed tables now in preview

    Lakehouse tables for Apache Iceberg are now in preview and available in the console. By using Google-managed Apache Iceberg tables in Lakehouse, you can eliminate the overhead of maintaining duplicate data pipelines and complex synchronization logic between BigQuery and open-source engines. This unified table format delivers native, multi-engine read and write interoperability, allowing you to run concurrent DML/DDL operations across diverse analytics tools on a single, shared storage layer.  Built-in automated table management handles painful background optimization tasks like compaction and partition tuning, freeing up your team to focus on building rather than managing storage maintenance.

June 1 - June 5

  • Beyond the Query: Powering AI Agents with Bigtable, Firestore & Memorystore

    Discover the latest advancements in Google Cloud's NoSQL Database portfolio, including Bigtable, Firestore, and Memorystore. This series is designed for a broad audience: whether you are exploring these databases for the first time or are an existing user looking to leverage the new capabilities announced at Next '26.

    Register here to secure your spot!

  • Cloud Engineer's AI Toolkit Workshops: Solve data-driven challenges with BigQuery, AlloyDB, Gemini and more. Hosted by Google Cloud Labs, this highly technical event is built specifically for Platform Engineers, SREs, and cloud infrastructure teams ready to bridge the gap between AI prototypes and production-grade deployments. Look out for more locations coming soon

    Toronto - June 25 (Data Cloud) | RSVP Here

    Chicago - June 30 (Data Cloud) | RSVP Here

  • Start a 10-day Bigtable free trial with a 1 node SSD cluster and up to 500GB of storage capacity. With no credit card required to start, you can easily ingest workloads and manage workloads that require low-latency, high-throughput, and predictable access. Plus, new Google Cloud customers get $300 in free credits on signup.

May 11 - May 15

  • Managed Service for Apache Airflow has launched a wave of new features, including the general availability of Airflow 3.1, AI-powered agentic troubleshooting, a new managed Airflow MCP Server for custom agent integration, and declarative YAML-based orchestration pipelines—discover all the details in the full blog post.

April 20 - April 24

  • Google-built ODBC Driver for BigQuery is now available in Preview

    We are excited to announce the launch of the new, Google-built ODBC driver for BigQuery. This new open-source driver provides a direct, high-performance connection for applications to BigQuery and is developed entirely in-house by Google.Download a new driver and connect your application to BigQuery.

April 13 - April 17

  • We announced we are reintroducing Data Studio to play a significant role in the AI era, expanding from data visualizations and reports to host BigQuery conversational agents and data apps built in Colab notebooks.
  • We announced BigQuery Graph is now available in preview, offering an easy-to-use, highly scalable graph analytics solution, empowering data professionals to model, analyze and visualize massive-scale relationships in an entirely new way.

April 6 - April 10

  • We introduced Conversational Analytics for Looker Embedded environments, enabling users to add natural language experiences to their own custom data-driven applications, powered by Gemini. 
  • We expanded Looker’s capabilities for faster ad-hoc analysis, with the introduction of self-service Explores, enabling you to bring your own data to Looker’s semantic layer and gain instant access to insights in a governed data environment.

March 23 - March 27

  • We showed you how you can scale your reads with Cloud SQL autoscaling read pools. This feature allows you to provision multiple read replicas that are accessible via a single read endpoint and to dynamically adjust your read capability based on real-time application needs. 
  • Our customers are leveraging the full power of Conversational Analytics and Looker to drive major business and technical breakthroughs in the AI era. Companies like Telenor, Pet Circle, Fluent Commerce, Lighthouse Intelligence, Wego, and ROLLER are turning data into insights and actions, grounded by Looker’s semantic layer.

March 16 - March 20

  • We introduced an enhanced Gemini assistant in BigQuery Studio, transforming the agent from a code assistant into a fully context-aware analytics partner.

February 23 - February 27

  • We introduced managed and remote MCP support for Google Cloud databases, including AlloyDB, Spanner, Cloud SQL, Bigtable and Firestore, to power the next generation of agents. This announcement extends the ability for AI models to plan, build, and solve complex problems, connecting to the database tools our customers leverage daily as the backbone of their work environment.

  • We outlined how you can build a conversational agent in BigQuery using the Conversational Analytics API to help you build context-aware agents that can understand natural language, query your BigQuery data, and deliver answers in text, tables, and visual charts.

February 16 - February 20

  • Our customers are leveraging the full power of Looker to drive major business and technical breakthroughs. Companies like Arrive, Audika, Carousell, Framebridge, GumGum, Intel, Overdose Digital, Ocean Network Express, Subskribe and Promevo are leveraging Looker’s newest AI-driven capabilities, including Conversational Analytics, to transform data to insights and actions, and empower their entire organization with a single source of truth, powered by Looker’s semantic layer.

February 2 - February 6

  • Join us on March 4 for our webinar, Win Your AI Strategy with Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus, to learn how to power your generative AI workloads with 3x higher performance and 99.99% availability. Register today to discover how to build a scalable, enterprise-grade foundation for your most demanding AI applications.

January 26 - January 30

  • We introduced Conversational Analytics in BigQuery, which allows users to analyze data using natural language. Conversational Analytics in BigQuery is an intelligent agent that generates, executes and visualizes answers grounded in your business context directly in BigQuery Studio, making data insights for data professionals more conversational.
  • We outlined how data products have become the foundation for AI agents, providing the context needed to make autonomous agents reliable and trusted for real business use, backed by organized business logic and semantic understanding.
  • We highlighted how you can supercharge data analytics workflows, and outlined Google Cloud’s AI agent offerings for data engineering, data science, and development tools, so you can integrate agentic workflows in your applications, empower your teams and speed discovery.

January 19 - January 23

  • We have fundamentally reimagined Firestore with pipeline operations for Enterprise edition. Experience a powerful new engine featuring over a hundred new query features, index-less queries, new index types, and observability tooling to improve query performance. Seamlessly migrate using built-in tools and leverage Firestore’s existing differentiated serverless foundation, virtually unlimited scale, and industry-leading SLA. Join a community of 600K developers to craft expressive applications that maximize the benefits of rich queryability, real-time listen queries, robust offline caching, and cutting-edge AI-assistive coding integrations.

  • Introducing Google Cloud SQL on MSSQLTips: We are highlighting a new technical guide published on MSSQLTips titled "Introducing Google Cloud SQL." This article serves as an essential resource for SQL Server administrators and developers exploring Google Cloud's fully managed database service. It provides a detailed overview of Cloud SQL capabilities, including high availability, security integration, and the seamless transition of on-premises SQL Server workloads to the cloud, making it an ideal resource for those planning their migration strategy.

  • We are excited to announce the Public Preview of Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) integration with Cloud SQL for SQL Server. Designed to tackle the challenge of identity sprawl in multi-cloud environments, this integration allows organizations to govern database access using their existing Microsoft identity infrastructure. Key benefits include centralized identity management, enhanced security features like Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), and simplified user administration through direct group mapping. This feature is available for SQL Server 2022 and supports both public and private IP configurations.

January 12 - January 16

  • Google-built JDBC Driver for BigQuery is now available in Preview

    We are excited to announce the launch of the new, Google-built JDBC driver for BigQuery. This new open-source driver provides a direct, high-performance connection for Java applications to BigQuery and is developed entirely in-house by Google.Download a new driver and connect your Java application to BigQuery.
  • Troubleshoot Airflow tasks instantly with Gemini Cloud Assist investigations: Cloud Composer just got smarter. We are excited to announce that Gemini Cloud Assist investigations are now available directly within Cloud Composer 3. Instead of manually sifting through raw logs, you can now simply click "Investigate" on a failed Airflow task. Gemini analyzes logs and task metadata to identify failure patterns—such as resource exhaustion or timeouts—and provides actionable recommendations driven by Gemini Cloud Assist to resolve the issue. This integration shifts the debugging experience from manual toil to automated root cause analysis, significantly reducing the time required to restore your pipelines. Learn more about AI-assisted troubleshooting.

Welcome to the second Cloud CISO Perspectives for October 2026. Today, Chris Betz talks with Michael Cote, our vulnerability rewards program lead, about the new tier of our Cloud VRP program and the current state of vulnerability rewards.

As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog. If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here.

Why we've created a new $250,000 tier for Google Cloud VRP (Q&A)

By Chris Betz, CISO, Google Cloud

The Google Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) partners with the global security research community to help elevate cloud security for all by encouraging the discovery of critical software vulnerabilities. In an era when automated research has made it more challenging to verify authentic vulnerabilities, we have a critical need to boost high-level, human-led research that can transcend automated-only discovery.

Today, we are expanding our top reward tier with a new $250,000 Root-in-Cloud reward, specifically designed to recognize high-impact architectural research. Identifying tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws requires human creativity, intuition, and rigorous systems analysis combined with the power of agentic systems.

To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of “roles/owner” or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup.

The exploit path can not depend on:

  • Pre-existing access or footholds in the victim project.
  • Leaked, phished, or stolen credentials.
  • User interaction or social engineering.

Proof-of-root: Clear, cryptographic validation

To make testing safe, clear, and reproducible, without impacting production environments, we have defined technical criteria for validating root-in-cloud access.

Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility.

Because code execution in Borg has the potential to impact service availability or cross-tenant data, researchers must halt all probing immediately upon achieving any execution in Borg. Escalation, extracting production credentials, and lateral movement are not allowed and will result in researcher disqualification.

The Google Cloud VRP panel will analyze the initial entry point, execution context, and attack surface to determine whether full arbitrary tenant or project takeover is achievable from that position, and award the bounty accordingly.

This new bounty tier reflects how security research continues to evolve, and the importance of continuing to recognize the most innovative and valuable security research. As part of those efforts, Google Security held its annual Escal8 conference in Singapore last week, and I had the opportunity to discuss the changing landscape with Michael Cote, Google Cloud’s vulnerability reward program lead.

The following transcript has been lightly edited.

Chris Betz: You are at Escal8 in Singapore announcing the new $250,000 Root-in-Cloud tier for our VRP. Why introduce this tier now, and what kind of research are you hoping to spark?

Michael Cote: This is a recognition of how the field of security research has changed over the past year. We value quality submissions from anyone, and we’ve seen that the combination of human creativity and agentic power is much richer than either on its own.

While automated scanners generate a high volume of low-impact noise, first-time researchers who pair human intuition with agentic tools are finding, on average, more interesting bugs than novices did two years ago. With the new Root-in-Cloud tier, we want to challenge the community and increasingly reward the complex, high-impact findings — like tenant-isolation bypasses and cross-service logic flaws — that require deep architectural intuition alongside agentic tools, because getting that information is essential to protecting our customers.

Chris Betz: Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) recently shared research showing that monthly CVE disclosures have doubled as agentic tools mature. From your seat leading the Cloud VRP, how has automation technology impacted the reports we’ve received? 

Michael Cote: It has transformed our intake volume, though not in the way many people assume. While the number of valid vulnerability reports submitted to the Google Cloud VRP has remained stable over the last 18 months, the total number of reports has grown tremendously.

Automation has helped democratize vulnerability discovery, and the barrier to entry has been rapidly flattening, something even our top researchers noted at Escal8. Because we’re seeing more researchers and more first-timers with interesting bugs, that creates pressure on more experienced researchers to move faster and bring more impactful findings — although their experience continues to be a key differentiator in success.

Chris Betz: I’ve been working with the research community for more than 20 years. One of the things I appreciate most is how much the community values making the world more secure. Bounty programs let us recognize this valuable work. How do you see the community changing as we move further into the agentic era?

Michael Cote: That shared commitment to making the world more secure is still the heart of this community, which is why the pressure to move faster is something we have to watch closely. As our GTIG colleagues found, the sharpest rise in the number of exploited vulnerabilities comes from n-days, not zero-days. 

Open source accounts have suggested that threat actors are using LLMs to rapidly turn newly-public vulnerability details into working exploits. When triage teams are already working through a surge in report volume, disclosing an unmitigated vulnerability well ahead of the standard 90-day coordinated disclosure window gives attackers the exact knowledge and time window they need to target customers.

With the influx of new submissions, I worry about a growing pressure to rush to publish. Something that concerns me because we’re already seeing early indications of it. Because LLMs lower the barrier to finding bugs in source-available software, researchers worry that waiting to verify risks will allow someone else to be first to publish. Even more concerning, that same competitive pressure can tempt even established security companies to disclose unmitigated vulnerabilities without coordination, and that rush puts our users directly at risk.

Project Zero helped establish the industry’s 90-plus-30-day responsible disclosure policy, and autonomous detection and exploitation capabilities make following coordinated disclosure more important than ever. In the long run, rushing to be first works against a security company's own self-interest. Novel discoveries may bring temporary visibility, but customers will ultimately choose not to work with organizations that put them and the broader ecosystem at risk. 

Chris Betz: When you offer a $250,000 bounty, how do you make sure researchers can validate their findings without putting customer environments or service availability at risk?

Michael Cote: High incentives require clear, safe rules of engagement. We never want researchers testing exploits against real customer projects. Instead, we created a deterministic proof-of-root mechanism using a designated service account. Researchers can cryptographically prove unauthorized access against that identity.

We’ve also updated our program rules to establish strict boundaries around underlying production infrastructure. If researchers think they are close to a breakthrough but are uncertain where the boundary lies, we encourage them to reach out. We are always more than happy to work with them to ensure they are recognized and rewarded for the value of their research without taking steps that would invalidate the bounty.

Chris Betz: What should enterprise CISOs take away from these trends? Especially those who run their own vulnerability management pipelines and partner with external researchers, what advice would you offer for navigating this AI inflection point?

Michael Cote: First, prepare your vulnerability triage workflows for agent-generated submissions. To keep valid reports from getting stuck in a backlog, security teams need ways to separate plausible-sounding hallucinations from real security risks.

Second, compress your remediation timelines once a vulnerability becomes public. Defensive patching and mitigations have to move faster because autonomous technology compresses the time from disclosure to working exploits.

Finally, hold your security partners and vendors to high standards of coordinated disclosure. It’s important that our industry continues to normalize agentic vulnerability research, but we must do so responsibly. Let’s continue to keep user safety at the center of everything we do.

For more information on the Google Cloud VRP, including detailed endpoint specifications, JSON payloads, and CLI examples, please check out our rules page.

In case you missed it

Here are the latest updates, products, services, and resources from our security teams so far this month:

  • How Google Does It: Using agents to help find, track, and fix vulnerabilities: Threat actors can now find software flaws faster than ever. To maintain an agile, responsive defense, we now use agentic systems with existing foundations. Read more.

  • How to use agents to stop insider threats: As agents find their place across the enterprise, we want to be sure that they neither become an insider threat nor enable people to become one. Read more.

  • Responding to core PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-10961: Follow these recommendations to minimize remote code execution risks in PHP from two critical vulnerabilities in the core PHP language runtime. Read more.

  • Wiz Sensor for GKE: Turnkey threat detection for Kubernetes: Introducing the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine in preview, helping to manage deployment, lifecycle, credential security, and governance. Read more.

  • Scale agents securely with IAM Helper Agent skills and MCP tools: Today we’re introducing IAM Helper, a suite of intelligent, agent-facing building blocks that can automate complex, end-to-end IAM workflows. Read more.

  • Introducing new scalable perimeter options with VPC Service Controls: Today, we're excited to announce key enhancements to VPC Service Controls that make perimeters easier to create, maintain, and scale. Read more.

  • Confidential G4 GPUs are now generally available: Confidential Computing on G4 now provides hardware-based security in AI Hypercomputer to deliver dynamic performance without compromising privacy. Read more.

  • Supply chain zero days: Closing the gap between publication and detection: Learn how Wiz’s supply chain pipeline identifies compromised packages at publication, helping teams detect zero-day supply chain compromises in Wiz Defend before a CVE is published. Read more.

Please visit the Google Cloud blog for more security stories published this month.

Threat Intelligence news

  • Investigating ephemeral supply chain tampering: For the first time, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with very short tampering windows that were active for only five to 10 minutes, and effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning. Read more.

  • ARMORY CASTLE exploits BeyondTrust: During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor, exploited a vulnerability impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances. Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public. Read more.

  • Vulnerability discovery and exploitation trends in the AI era: To counter the increased risk from rapid vulnerability discovery and exploitation, organizations should transition from unprioritized mass-patching to threat intelligence-driven triage, combining targeted edge-defense with automated, agentic remediation. Read more.

  • Defending against active exploitation of Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances: Mandiant Consulting and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified active, in-the-wild exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances. Here’s our containment and remediation guidance. Read more.

Please visit the Google Cloud blog for more threat intelligence stories published this month.

Now hear this: Podcasts from Google Cloud

  • Cloud Security Podcast: Patching browsers with AI, agents, Rust, and your tabs: Jasika Bawa and Doug Turner of Chrome Security explore how Google Chrome now uses AI agents to autonomously identify and patch security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale, significantly accelerating the browser's update cadence. Listen here.

entries.content:
Pramod Niralakeri

Strategic Cloud Engineer

Enterprise organizations often leverage multiple data platforms, including Databricks, to execute heavy Apache Spark jobs alongside BigQuery to power highly concurrent analytics workloads. Historically, bridging these systems often meant building complex pipelines to copy data between environments. This approach increases storage costs, introduces latency, and fragments security controls.

With Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse, you can now query Databricks-managed Apache Iceberg tables straight from BigQuery. This zero-copy approach removes the need to duplicate data: BigQuery reads the same files Databricks writes, and new changes appear after Lakehouse's next scheduled metadata refresh (as often as every 5 minutes).

How Lakehouse and Databricks work together

Managed Iceberg tables automatically generates Iceberg-compatible metadata alongside native Delta logs. Data engineering teams can store Parquet files once in Google Cloud Storage (GCS) using Databricks. Rather than loading this information into BigQuery, Lakehouse reads the Iceberg metadata directly, applying BigQuery’s vectorized engine directly to open-format files in GCS.

Although Google Cloud Storage (GCS) serves as the primary storage layer in the above example, Lakehouse extends this borderless federation directly to external cloud environments like Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage. By pairing the open Apache Iceberg REST Catalog with cross-cloud connections, Lakehouse lets BigQuery query data across clouds without moving it. Each federated catalog lives in a Google Cloud location you choose, ideally the region closest to your data. This lets BigQuery read open-format Parquet files where they live, delivering multi-cloud analytics without replication pipelines. Remote-cloud egress charges still apply, but Cross-Cloud Interconnect (AWS) and Lakehouse caching can reduce them.

Beyond simply querying external data, Lakehouse framework establishes true read and write (R/W) interoperability across engines. Because the platform is built on an open Apache Iceberg foundation, data teams can effortlessly execute multi-statement SQL commands directly inside BigQuery.

Centralized security and governance

Handling access controls across disparate systems can introduce vulnerabilities. Lakehouse addresses this through delegated access. Administrators can configure a BigQuery Cloud Resource Connection tied to a service account that manages IAM rights for GCS buckets. Granting users access to the Lakehouse table entity lets you enforce BigQuery controls including row-level, column-level security, and dynamic data masking on external Iceberg tables while Databricks handles ingestion.

Catalog federation and credential vending

Previously, connecting these platforms meant manually configuring BigQuery queries to point at static metadata paths. Modern setups leverage the open Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API. Databricks Unity Catalog functions as the central metadata layer, allowing a BigQuery administrator to establish a Lakehouse runtime catalog with a federated connection. When running a query, Lakehouse contacts Unity Catalog for current table state, and short-lived tokens are issued through credential vending to grant BigQuery temporary read access to GCS.

Partition pruning

BigQuery uses each table's Iceberg metadata to plan the query, then reads only the relevant data files in place. Iceberg's hidden partitioning lets you filter on logical columns, such as timestamps, without knowing the directory layout. Note that Databricks managed Iceberg tables don't support partition transforms; Databricks recommends liquid clustering instead.

Filters in a standard WHERE clause let BigQuery use the Iceberg manifests to skip partitions that can't match. Compare partition columns with literal values so pruning can apply. These manifests maintain detailed column-level statistical bounds, enabling BigQuery to bypass irrelevant manifest records and unneeded Parquet files immediately. Consequently, queries scan only necessary byte ranges, accelerating query execution while significantly reducing on-demand slot consumption and storage scan costs.

Fast queries with Iceberg metadata and Lakehouse caching

Iceberg manifests already identify which data files to read, so BigQuery doesn't need a metadata cache for Iceberg tables. For cross-cloud tables, such as those in Amazon S3, Lakehouse caching (Preview) keeps retrieved data blocks in Google Cloud so repeat queries read them locally. BigQuery reads the Iceberg manifest files directly when it plans each query; there's no metadata caching to enable. This dynamic partition pruning bypasses unneeded files, significantly reducing runtime and bytes scanned.

Maintenance and lifecycle management

Modern lakehouses demand active upkeep; without routine care, performance degrades into an inefficient repository. Fortunately, both BigQuery and Databricks supply native capabilities to preserve table hygiene and accelerate analytical workloads.

Keeping your tables optimized

To maintain optimal query performance, active maintenance of your lakehouse storage footprint remains necessary.

  • Trigger regular compaction pipelines via Databricks APIs to merge tiny Parquet files into larger, optimized layouts and use Predictive Optimization.

  • Execute the Databricks VACUUM command to clear unreferenced files outside active snapshots, avoiding extra GCS storage costs.

Compaction and the small file problem

Frequent write operations, continuous ingestion jobs, and streaming workloads continuously produce thousands of small Parquet files. This fragmentation creates a storage bottleneck that can limit BigQuery’s reading efficiency. Establishing thousands of network connections to GCS and processing metadata footers across numerous tiny files consumes significant compute time, diminishing the performance advantages of vectorized query execution.

Running routine compaction within Iceberg resolves these inefficiencies. Databricks manages this automatically using Liquid Clustering which dynamically adjusts file layouts based on access patterns or through native table management utilities.

To compact small files manually on Databricks, run OPTIMIZE:

Executing this command aggregates scattered file segments into larger, structured blocks typically between 256MB and 512MB that can help improve BigQuery’s scan throughput. The binpack approach operates rapidly by prioritizing total file size balancing, though alternative sorting strategies can organize dataset ordering along specific column keys.

Managing orphan files and snapshot retention (VACUUM)

Every transactional update, record modification, and table compaction creates fresh snapshots within Iceberg to preserve dataset integrity. Over time, historical Parquet objects detached from active table states become orphaned. Although these legacy files facilitate time-travel analytics, neglecting them can drive up GCS storage charges over time.

Data teams can use the Databricks VACUUM operation to scan and purge abandoned storage files.

Standard configurations apply a mandatory seven-day threshold (deletedFileRetentionDuration) before executing VACUUM routines. Preserving this delay prevents active analytical jobs from encountering missing file errors while keeping historical recovery options available. Scheduling routine VACUUM jobs, or letting predictive optimization run them, removes unreferenced data files and, for tables with Iceberg reads, old Iceberg metadata. That keeps storage costs low and performance high across your lakehouse.

Conclusion

Connecting Databricks Apache Iceberg datasets to Lakehouse can help you activate your data with BigQuery. By separating processing from underlying storage, embracing open formats, and using standard REST APIs with credential vending, you can run scalable engineering workloads and concurrent analytics without migrating data or sacrificing performance

Pairing Databricks Iceberg reads (UniForm) with Lakehouse federation, Lakehouse caching, and regular OPTIMIZE and VACUUM maintenance helps you build an efficient, zero-copy lakehouse. This approach can help lower storage spend, avoids fragile pipeline maintenance, and prepares your data environment for modern analytics and emerging AI workloads.

Constructing a unified architecture no longer requires moving data files across platforms. You can begin querying Databricks Iceberg tables by registering them with the Lakehouse runtime catalog today for bi-directional federation. Learn more by reading our documentation to get started.

entries.content:
Maggy Hu

Product Manager

Paulina Trzeciak

Product Manager

Picture the scene: Before an executive business review, your VP of Sales asks an AI assistant, "What was net revenue for our top enterprise accounts last quarter?" In seconds, the agent returns a polished chart! Unfortunately, the numbers don't match the finance report. Why? Because the agent counted cancelled orders as revenue and pulled from an unvalidated staging table.

The agent didn't fail because of the model, or because it couldn't translate a user question into a query. It failed because it didn't understand your business. The real kicker is that understanding usually already exists in the form of a semantic model in a Looker, dbt, Snowflake, Databricks, or SAP system. But because each definition stays locked inside its own tool, every agent guesses at it… and often gets it wrong.

This is where Knowledge Catalog comes in. It brings the semantic models from all of those tools into one context graph, so every agent works from the same trusted definitions. And when two tools define the same metric differently, both definitions appear with their provenance, so data stewards can reconcile the conflict before it reaches end users.

Today, we're announcing the general availability of expanded semantic model support. Knowledge Catalog now natively ingests semantic models and metric definitions from Looker LookML, BigQuery Graph (including BigQuery measures), dbt MetricFlow, Snowflake Semantic Views, Databricks Metric Views, and SAP Core Schema Notation (CSN), and connects them with schema, lineage, data profiles, business glossary and other key metadata in a single context graph, without moving data or rewriting business logic in a new language.

By grounding your AI agents in those models, they get the same business definitions your analysts rely on, so their answers line up with the numbers your business trusts. In fact, based on internal benchmarks, grounding agents in Knowledge Catalog makes them nearly 4X more accurate, with up to 33% lower latency, and using up to 75% fewer tokens.

The unified context graph enables you to:

  • Reuse the semantic models you already trust: Knowledge Catalog grounds Gemini agent, BigQuery Conversational Analytics, and your custom agents in the metrics, filters, and join paths your teams have already defined, wherever they live.

  • Go beyond hand-curated definitions with self-learned context: Knowledge Catalog pairs the well-defined metrics and KPI definitions in your semantic models with relevant context it extracts from unstructured knowledge sources, such as operational playbooks, meeting notes, chat threads, code, and more. Powered by Gemini, self-learning enrichment continuously finds missing or outdated context and turns it into governed, reusable context sets, ensuring your agents' context stays current as definitions change, without relying only on manual curation.

  • Pair business logic with enterprise trust: Even the right formula produces the wrong answer when it runs on stale or uncertified data. That's why Knowledge Catalog can connect semantic definition to data quality scores, freshness signals, and lineage, so an agent knows what it can trust before it writes a line of SQL.

Side-by-side comparison of the same question in Gemini without Knowledge Catalog (left) and grounded in Knowledge Catalog (right). Highlights the grounded agent (right) giving an accurate response with less token and lower latency, compared to the agent without Knowledge Catalog (left) hallucinating and using more tokens with higher latency.

One context graph across your data estate

The context graph that Knowledge Catalog creates is a connected map of your data and semantic estate: tables, semantic models, glossary terms, and data products are nodes; lineage, associations, schema keys, joins mined from real query history, and the join paths declared in your semantic models are the edges. Ingested semantics land in that same graph, next to pre-existing governance and usage signals, so an agent moves from business concept to trusted formula and verified join paths in one traversal. Each source adds its own perspective on your business:

  • Looker LookML (GA): Indexes models, explores, views, and dashboards using Live sync from Looker Core, capturing compiled metric SQL, fan-out-safe join conditions, mandatory filters, and lineage from source tables to executive dashboards.

  • BigQuery Graph (GA): Indexes native property-graph definitions, node and edge tables, graph measures, and business synonyms, so agents reason over connected entities with Graph Query Language (GQL) traversals instead of brittle multi-table self-joins.

  • dbt MetricFlow (GA): Links source objects to dbt models and MetricFlow metrics, alongside dbt data quality test results, filters, saved queries, freshness SLAs, and downstream exposures.

  • Snowflake Semantic Views via Horizon Catalog (GA): Pairs federated BigQuery or Google Cloud Lakehouse tables with Snowflake Horizon metadata, bringing in Semantic View dimensions, facts, metric formulas, relationships, and synonyms, plus Data Metric Function quality scorecards and PII masking tags.
  • Databricks Metric Views via Unity Catalog (GA): Ingests metric view definitions, measure formulas, scoping filters, and join cardinalities from Unity Catalog, alongside table certification badges and Lakehouse Monitoring profiling results.

  • SAP Core Schema Notation (CSN) via SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) (GA): Captures business labels, dimension and cube modeling patterns, default aggregations, currency and unit bindings, key and composite join associations, and data sensitivity flags when SAP BDC Data Products are federated through Google Cloud Lakehouse.

Because every source lands as a node or an edge in the same graph, a LookML join, a dbt exposure, a Snowflake relationship, or an SAP association are traversable side by side, with links tying each one back to the physical tables it depends on. And nothing is silently overwritten: overlapping definitions stay side by side, each labeled with its source, giving data stewards the full picture they need to settle on a single version.

Navigating semantic models, join paths, and lineage on the context graph in Knowledge Studio.

You can explore and govern all of this in Knowledge Studio (preview), your command center to explore and manage your context. Explore your context graph, including your semantic definitions, using natural language prompts and traverse connection paths using the context graph canvas. Then, once you've validated the right assets and definitions, you can package them into reusable context sets that map to specific use cases and domains in your organization, which Gemini and custom agents can consume in production.

Get started

Let’s get back to that net revenue question. With Knowledge Catalog, the VP of Sales’ agent issues a single context query to discover the trusted asset, applying the exact metric formula and filters that your domain experts defined, all while respecting join keys across systems, and confirming that the underlying data passed its quality checks. Better yet, the numbers in the report are correct!

To get started, explore your context graph in Knowledge Studio and visit the Knowledge Catalog documentation to connect to more sources.

entries.content:
Omkar Deshmukh

Product Manager

Josh Choinsky

Software Engineer

Managing PostgreSQL databases across on-premises, edge, and multi-cloud environments often forces administrators to rely on command-line tools, making it hard to see cluster health and quickly diagnose issues. To solve this, we are announcing the General Availability (GA) of the AlloyDB Omni Web UI for Red Hat and containers. This production-ready, read-only console gives you direct visibility into hardware telemetry, query performance, and configuration flags for AlloyDB Omni so you can troubleshoot workloads quickly and safely without leaving your local or enterprise environment.

What is AlloyDB Omni?

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, self-managed edition of AlloyDB that brings enterprise capabilities and full PostgreSQL compatibility to your own infrastructure. Built to run anywhere — across on-premises data centers, edge environments, and multi-cloud deployments — it includes built-in columnar acceleration and integrated AI tooling. With AlloyDB Omni, you can modernize demanding transactional and analytical workloads while retaining complete control over your operating environment.

Key Web UI capabilities at a glance

  • Cluster overview and profiles: Switch between target connection profiles quickly without using the command line.

  • System monitoring: View real-time performance telemetry for CPU, memory, and disk I/O to plan capacity and triage infrastructure issues.

  • Query performance: Identify resource-heavy SQL statements through a visual breakdown of database load, latency bottlenecks, and slow queries.

  • Columnar Engine diagnostics: Track the in-memory columnar store, caching, and coverage to verify analytical query acceleration.

  • Parameter and flag auditing: Inspect runtime database parameters centrally to identify configuration drift against your organizational baselines.

  • AlloyDB AI and ecosystem shortcuts: Inspect vector search and AI workflows, and access quick launchpad shortcuts for ecosystem tools like pgBackRest.

Production-safe diagnostics and profile management

When you triage complex database workloads across bare-metal VMs, containers, or Kubernetes, you need a clear, isolated view of instance health. The Web UI provides a dedicated visual environment for this.

  • Profile management: Store and toggle between saved connection profiles for local development, staging, or production environments.

  • Read-only operations: The interface operates strictly in read-only mode, ensuring that diagnostic sessions cannot execute write commands or modify your underlying database configurations.

Dual-layer observability: System and query monitoring

To isolate production performance spikes, you need immediate visibility into both hardware health and SQL statement execution.

  • System monitoring: The Web UI integrates with standard Prometheus telemetry to show you real-time CPU use, memory allocation, storage I/O, and active connection trends.

  • Query monitoring: The dashboard automatically ranks execution-heavy SQL statements by total latency and call frequency. You can instantly isolate unindexed or resource-intensive queries to resolve issues faster.

System Insights and Query Insights in AlloyDB Omni Web UI

Real-time Columnar Engine diagnostics

AlloyDB Omni includes an advanced Columnar Engine that organizes frequently accessed data in memory, accelerating analytical queries significantly compared to standard PostgreSQL. The Web UI helps you monitor this feature directly:

  • Memory footprint tracking: Check real-time columnar memory consumption against your hardware limits.

  • Columnarization and cache coverage: See exactly which tables and columns are actively cached in memory to confirm your workloads are running as fast as possible.

AlloyDB AI and Columnar Engine Insights in AlloyDB Omni Web UI

Database flag and parameter auditing

Keeping database parameters uniform across distributed environments keeps your operations stable. The Web UI gives you a central catalog to inspect active database flags and runtime settings. You can verify node settings against your organizational policies without connecting to servers via SSH or parsing configuration files manually. If configuration drift is detected, changes should be applied via the authoritative provisioning workflow (e.g., updating Kubernetes CRDs/GitOps manifests, running Ansible playbooks, or using alloydbctl).

Database flags in AlloyDB Omni Web UI

Built-in AlloyDB AI and tooling hub

As you build generative AI applications on top of PostgreSQL, the Web UI gives you direct visibility into vector search workflows and AI model integrations. You can also quickly navigate to documentation and external ecosystem resources, including backup tools like pgBackRest, directly from the console's tooling hub.

Operational scope and prerequisites

We designed the AlloyDB Omni Web UI with clear operational boundaries so you can deploy it easily within enterprise security boundaries and air-gapped environments.

  • Non-Intrusive Monitoring: The interface operates with minimal permissions out of the box, preserving your existing command-line tools and CI/CD pipelines as the authoritative controls for cluster provisioning and administrative workflows.

  • Standard monitoring prerequisites: To see complete system hardware metrics, you need standard Prometheus monitoring configured within your host environment.

Get started

Ready to modernize your PostgreSQL workloads and get dedicated observability for your AlloyDB Omni cluster ?

  • Sign up for enterprise access:

  • To request access to RPM-based enterprise distributions, advanced tooling, and the Web UI, complete the sign-up form for RPM based deployment of AlloyDB Omni.

  • To request access to container-based enterprise distributions, advanced tooling, and the Web UI, complete the sign-up form for container-based deployment.

  • Install the Web UI: Follow the step-by-step installation instructions in the AlloyDB Omni documentation to deploy the AlloyDB Omni Web UI

  • For deployment using Red Hat RPM: Deploy via native RPM Package

  • For deployment using Docker or Podman: Deploy via container image

You can adopt similar
entries.content:
Remigiusz Samborski

Lead Developer Relations Engineer

In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills, covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates that every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons that we learned along the way. You can adopt similar gates and review rules in your own skill repository.

Since my last post, the Google Agent Skills repository has passed 21,000 GitHub stars, up from 15,000. It now hosts over 170 skills from teams across Google, and we distribute them across multiple AI platforms.

Building agent skills for a single developer or a small project is straightforward. You write a 

SKILL.md
file, define a few instructions, test it manually, and it works. At our scale, manual workflows stop being effective. Unvetted edits can introduce subtle bugs, and it becomes difficult to catch issues before they reach users.

The core philosophy: Ship skills like products

One key lesson from my previous post: a skill is a living product, not a one-off document. In practice, that means we ship every skill update like a product release.

It's tempting to treat a skill as documentation. But documentation explains concepts to a human reader, while a skill steers an AI agent's reasoning loop, tool selection, and execution path. A misplaced phrase in a skill can cause an agent to invoke invalid command flags, enter an infinite loop, or waste tokens.

That makes every instruction edit a behavioral change. You wouldn't ship a product update without testing it, and the same goes for a skill. This principle drives three core requirements:

  • Strict semantic versioning: Every behavioral change requires an explicit version bump.

  • Deterministic automated validation: Linters and validators check every proposed change before a human or AI reviewer sees it.

  • Mandatory evaluation evidence: Every change includes an evaluation report. It compares the skill against its previous version, or—if the skill is new—against an agent without the skill.

Automated conformance gates: The pull request pipeline

In my previous post, I briefly listed the checks that every skill passes on check-in: linters, link checkers, and AI-assisted checklists. Here's what's inside them, plus two gates that I haven't covered before: semantic versioning and evaluation suite validation.

When an author submits a change to our internal skills repository, an automated continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline triggers immediately. Before a skill is exported to GitHub, it must pass these six automated gates and receive human approval:

  • Structural conformance: Directory layout, allowed files, and taxonomy.

  • Skill linters: Frontmatter, folder naming, and Markdown rules.

  • Semantic versioning: Version bump for every behavioral change.

  • Evaluation suite: Valid eval suite and a fresh eval report.

  • Link validation: Links are valid.

  • AI review agent: Skill quality and design standards.

  • Human approval: Final approval from a human reviewer (a subject matter expert).

Structural conformance and skill linters

Our automated validation suite inspects every pull request for structural and syntactical correctness. Some of the rules include these requirements:

  • Folder name and metadata name must match.

  • SKILL.md
    and description length limits are enforced.

  • All required fields in the frontmatter 

    metadata
    are present.

  • Only a curated list of files and directories is allowed within a skill directory.

  • All Markdown files follow formatting rules.

  • The main 

    README.md
    file and the machine-readable 
    index.json
    registry are up to date.

Semantic versioning

Every skill declares a semantic version in its 

SKILL.md
frontmatter metadata:

First, our automated checks verify that the version is a quoted string. YAML parses unquoted values like 

2.0
as numbers, which causes unexpected parsing errors in tools that expect a string.

Second, the validator checks the version transition itself. New skills must start at 

1.0.0
, and any change to an existing skill's instructions, scripts, or references requires a version bump or the pull request is blocked. Standard reset rules apply: bumping 
MAJOR
(for example, 
1.4.2
to 
2.0.0
) resets 
MINOR
and 
PATCH
to 
0
, and bumping 
MINOR
(for example, 
1.4.2
to 
1.5.0
) resets 
PATCH
to 
0
.

Why enforce strict versioning if the agent only reads the Markdown instructions? The version number is for the developer and their package tooling, not for the model at runtime. Skills don't auto-update in the background, which means there's no network check or latency overhead each time an agent invokes a skill. Instead, explicit versions let developers compare their locally installed skills against the upstream catalog and decide when to pull changes—for example, by running the 

npx skills update
command. This versioning also supports workflows where teams want to lock a critical skill to a known-good version to guarantee reproducible agent behavior across their projects.

Evaluation suite validation

Our continuous evaluations (evals) compare agent performance with and without each skill. Those results are only as reliable as the evaluation suites behind them. If a suite contains broken file references or compound expectations, test results become noisy and untrustworthy.

Our validator parses each evaluation suite and the pull request description. Then it checks several strict invariants:

  • Resolution of file-based prompts: When a test prompt references a file (such as 

    @file:test_prompt.txt
    ), the validator confirms that the target file exists and that it isn't empty.

  • Atomic expectations: Each expectation must check exactly one criterion. The validator blocks compound expectations until authors split them. Lesson 2 later in this post shows why.

  • Duplicate detection: The validator flags duplicate test prompts and conflicting expectations within the same evaluation suite.

  • Mandatory evaluation report: Every pull request that modifies a skill must link to an evaluation report in its description.

  • Eval staleness check: Authors usually iterate on a pull request as reviewers leave feedback. The validator confirms that the linked report ran against the latest commit.

Link validation

Over 170 skills link to documentation for fast-evolving Google products, and those pages can move long after a skill passes review. Rather than waiting for users to report broken links, we validate links at two stages. Before merge, pull request checks verify all relative links, such as files in 

references/
.

Then, every Monday, a GitHub Actions workflow runs lychee across all external links in the public repository and it reports any broken links to skill owners for remediation.

AI review agent

Linters and schema validators catch syntactic errors, but they can't evaluate overall quality. They can't tell you if an instruction is confusing, if a reference guide is too verbose, or if a task should have been a bash script instead of a large language model (LLM) instruction.

To solve this, we integrated an AI review agent into our review pipeline. When a change affects a skill, the AI reviewer inspects it using a dedicated review skill. Yes, we use a skill to review skills.

Here are the core rules the AI reviewer evaluates. You can adopt these rules in your own skill development workflows.

1. Skill suitability and the deterministic trap

The first question our AI reviewer asks is simple: Does this task belong in an instruction?

We often see authors fall into the deterministic trap. They write rigid, numbered sequences of command-line interface (CLI) commands directly into Markdown text.

LLMs are probabilistic engines. If an operation requires a strict sequence of commands where a variation can cause an error, embedding those commands in the instruction text invites hallucinations.

Our AI reviewer enforces a clear boundary between deterministic and probabilistic logic. Rigid CLI sequences, JSON parsers, and deployment steps must live in executable scripts under 

scripts/
. Markdown instructions are reserved for tasks that require judgment, such as choosing an architecture, diagnosing error logs, or synthesizing code.

This rule complements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) guidance that I shared last time: prefer remote MCP tools whenever possible. When you must fall back to CLI or API calls, wrap them in a script instead of spelling them out in the instructions.

2. The L1/L2/L3 modular architecture

Context windows are valuable. Loading a 2,000-line skill into an agent consumes context and degrades reasoning.

Our AI reviewer enforces a three-tier information hierarchy that follows the progressive disclosure model of Agent Skills:

  • Level 1 (Metadata): The YAML frontmatter (

    name
    , 
    description
    ). The agent uses this concise summary for discovery and routing.

  • Level 2 (Core instructions): The main 

    SKILL.md
    file. The body must stay compact (under 500 lines). It provides workflow overviews, decision trees, and guardrails.

  • Level 3 (Reference docs): Detailed API references, schemas, and other reference tables live in a 

    references/
    directory.

Our AI reviewer enforces two distinct rules for Level 3: flat directory structure and single-hop indirection. Keeping 

references/
flat (no subdirectories) is a repository convention that discourages sprawling documentation trees and makes file discovery simpler. More importantly for runtime performance, the reviewer blocks chained references, where 
SKILL.md
links to a reference file that links to yet another file. Each hop requires an extra tool call, adding latency and cost, and our evaluations showed that agents frequently stop before following a second level of chained references.

3. Non-interactive script design

When skills bundle helper scripts in 

scripts/
, we expect agents to execute them directly in terminal sandboxes.

Our AI reviewer flags any script that blocks on interactive prompts. Every script must accept inputs through command-line flags or environment variables, provide 

--help
documentation, and include a 
--dry-run
or confirmation flag for destructive operations. Scripts also need to separate output cleanly, writing structured data (usually JSON) to standard output and writing actionable error messages to standard error.

Example AI review checklist snippet

The review skill also checks frontmatter for spec compliance and discovery, and it turns the L1/L2/L3 architecture into concrete structure rules. Here's an excerpt from those criteria:

Human approval

After it passes all automated checks, every pull request must receive approval from a human reviewer. The reviewer is typically the skill's subject matter expert and, for new skills, a member of the Central Skills team.

Lessons learned from repository history

Six months of commit history and pull request discussions reveal several practical takeaways.

1. Scope CI checks carefully

Early in the project, we configured automated pull request checks with broad directory patterns.

One check required an approved bug tracking ticket on every change. Because the pattern matched too broadly, engineers making a one-line typo fix were blocked for missing a tracking ticket. Meanwhile, newly added skills in deeper subdirectories went uninspected.

Takeaway: Match automated check rules to specific file operations, such as added versus modified files, and verify exact path depths. Treat minor edits to existing skills differently from new skills.

2. Atomic expectations

When we started writing evaluation suites, we saw authors write compound expectations like this:

If the agent configured the region and lifecycle rules but missed the uniform access flag, the LLM-as-a-judge scorer returned inconsistent ratings.

Migrating to atomic expectations resolved the inconsistent ratings:

Takeaway: Check exactly one criterion per expectation. Atomic expectations make evaluation results clear, reliable, and debuggable.

3. Documentation drift happens fast

In a multi-contributor repository, documentation tables drift within days if maintained manually.

Takeaway: If you publish an index or catalog, never rely on contributors to update it manually. Instead, write a generator script and enforce it with a CI unit test. That's the origin of the 

README.md
and 
index.json
checks in our linters. Our 
index.json
even opens with a warning: "This file is generated. Do not edit it by hand."

4. Gate expensive LLM checks behind fast deterministic ones

Running full evaluation suites and an AI review agent on every change can get expensive fast, both in token usage and CI runtime—especially when authors push frequent small commits during review.

In our pipeline, fast deterministic checks run first. Structural conformance, skill linters, and semantic versioning act as blocking gates: if any of them fail, the pipeline stops immediately and it won't trigger the AI reviewer or evaluation checks until those issues are fixed.

Takeaway: Stage your pipeline so cheap, deterministic checks block broken changes before LLM-powered gates run. When you build a similar system, consider adding further cost guardrails, such as manual triggers for heavy checks (for example, a 

/run-evals
pull request comment) or only triggering automatic re-runs when the diff exceeds a specific threshold.

Conclusion

Building a scalable Agent Skills repository requires more than good prompt engineering. It requires solid developer infrastructure:

  • Ship skills like products: version, validate, and evaluate every change.

  • Enforce semantic versioning and atomic expectations with automated CI gates.

  • Use an AI reviewer to catch design anti-patterns, such as the deterministic trap.

  • Check links before merge and on a schedule.

Links and further reading

  • Google Agent Skills repo: github.com/google/skills

  • Previous post: Behind the scenes: How we build, test, and scale Google Agent Skills

  • Launch announcement: Level Up Your Agents: Announcing Google's Official Skills Repository

  • Skills tutorial: Introduction: What Are Google Cloud Agent Skills?

What's next?
